crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: High-Frequency Market Microstructure
children.blurb: High-frequency market microstructure is the study of how orders are submitted, matched, and priced over very short time horizons, from milliseconds down to microseconds.

children.name: Non-Linear Factor Models
children.blurb: Non-linear factor models extend traditional factor investing by allowing the relationship between factors and asset returns to bend, interact, or change with market conditions.

children.name: Learning Trade Execution
children.blurb: Learning trade execution is the use of machine learning to decide how, when, and where to place orders in financial markets.

children.name: Statistical Arbitrage
children.blurb: Statistical arbitrage is a quantitative trading approach that looks for relative value between related securities, often using statistical models to identify temporary mispricings.

children.name: Detecting Market Regime Shifts
children.blurb: Detecting market regime shifts means identifying when the statistical behavior of a market changes, such as moving from low volatility to high volatility or from trending to mean reverting.

sections.body: Quantitative trading uses mathematical and statistical models to make trading decisions, often at speeds and scales beyond human discretion. AI enters through pattern recognition, nonlinear prediction, reinforcement learning for execution, and unsupervised detection of changing market conditions. In practice, models ingest order book data, trade prints, quotes, news, and alternative data to forecast short horizon returns or optimal order placement. The work is not a single algorithm but a pipeline: data cleaning, feature construction, signal generation, portfolio construction, risk controls, and execution. AI is also used to simulate market impact and to learn policies that trade a large order without moving the price too much. The field overlaps with market microstructure, factor investing, statistical arbitrage, and regime detection.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Execution algorithms that slice orders and adapt to liquidity are widely deployed, and linear factor models remain standard for risk decomposition. Machine learning has improved short term forecasting in some settings, especially where data is abundant and the signal is weak but persistent. What is not solved: financial data is noisy, non stationary, and low signal to noise, so overfitting is a constant danger. Regime shifts can break a model overnight, and backtests often fail to capture crowding, latency, or market impact. Honest limits include limited historical data for rare events, unclear causality, and the difficulty of distinguishing a real edge from data mining, and the site tracks 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices, which gives a narrow but concrete view of how AI themed assets trade, not a full picture of all quantitative strategies.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages under this section build from market plumbing to model design to execution and adaptation. High-Frequency Market Microstructure explains the order book, latency, and the mechanics that any short horizon model must respect. Non-Linear Factor Models covers how AI extends traditional factor investing with interactions and nonlinear exposures. Learning Trade Execution focuses on reinforcement learning and other methods for placing orders, minimizing impact, and adapting to liquidity. Statistical Arbitrage describes relative value strategies that seek mean reversion or mispricing across related instruments. Detecting Market Regime Shifts addresses the problem of knowing when the statistical properties of the market have changed, which is often the difference between a working model and a broken one, and a reader would go to each page for a specific layer of the quantitative trading stack, from microstructure to factors to execution to arbitrage to regime awareness.
